newsitem.title: JAPAN: Cambodia's aid donors draw line in sand.
newsitem.headline: Cambodia's aid donors draw line in sand.

text.p: Japan and other major aid donors to Cambodia have drawn a line in the sand with their assistance which Phnom Penh's new rulers risk crossing at their peril.
Behind the diplomatic posturing both inside and outside Cambodia about the recent government upheaval in Phnom Penh is a clear signal for the country's new sole ruler Hun Sen.

Major aid donor nations, while unhappy at the violence, have signalled that they are prepared to live with what has happened so far, as long as peace and freedoms are quickly restored, general elections take place next year and there is no further witchhunt for political foes.

"If Hun Sen crosses those lines, the least that will happen is that the aid carpet will be pulled out from under him completely," an authoritative source said in Japan, the biggest aid donor to Cambodia.
Cambodia gets half its annual budget from overseas donations, with Japan by far the biggest contributor, sending nearly half of the aid amount.

Japanese officials have so far adopted the most low-key approach of all major donors to the events in Cambodia in which Hun Sen unseated his co-prime minister Prince Norodom Ranariddh to take sole control of the country.
Tokyo maintains it has neither cut off aid to Cambodia nor threatened to cut off aid.
A Japanese official said if there had been disruptions in aid it has simply been because turmoil in Cambodia had made it impossible to get supplies to where they are needed.

In contrast, the United States has frozen its aid for the moment to Cambodia, and Australia announced on Tuesday it was halting military aid while leaving alone A$32 million (US$23.7 million) a year in general aid.
The Japanese official said Tokyo's view was that fighting that broke out between Hun Sen and Ranariddh was a domestic political struggle in Cambodia.
Some Japanese officials have even suggested that Ranariddh might have only himself to blame for the conflict because he was planning a similar move against Hun Sen but lost out.
Hun Sen has accused Ranariddh of trying to infiltrate Khmer Rouge forces into the capital to bolster the prince's strength so that he could move against Hun Sen.
The Khmer Rouge, led by Pol Pot, ruled Cambodia from 1975 to 1978, when some two million Cambodians died through persecution, murder or starvation in the so-called "Killing Fields".
If major aid donors have sent a signal to Hun Sen of grudging acceptance of what has happened, a different message has gone out to the prince.

The prince has so far pleaded his case in meetings with French and Japanese envoys in Paris, U.N. Secretary-General Kofi Annan in New York, and U.S. State Department officials and members of Congress in Washington, as well as in telephone calls to leaders from the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN).
But apart from a sympathetic hearing and advice to try to make peace with Hun Sen, the prince has received no firm offers of support to undo what has happened.
Japanese officials have even pointed to a weekend statement on the crisis by the prince's father, King Norodom Sihanouk, as a sign that the monarch also accepts the "victorious" new regime.

In the statement, the 74-year-old king who is ill in Beijing, said he would "not oppose" the signing of decrees and laws validating a reconstituted coalition government once it receives a vote of confidence from the National Assembly.
The King's words were almost an echo of what major aid donors want -- an adherence to the 1991 Paris Accords which brought peace to Cambodia.
